prize_parts.citation: for the optical detection and coherent control of single electron spins of nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond at room temperature

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B001 as my preferred configuration, with the same two names and the same narrow citation. The question I ask of every candidate is whether we can name the original experiment and the people who did it, and whether anyone can repeat it today. For B001 the answer is unusually concrete: the optical detection of a single nitrogen-vacancy centre in diamond (Wrachtrup group, 1997) and the coherent manipulation of its electron and nuclear spin at room temperature (Jelezko and Wrachtrup, 2004). These are tabletop experiments reproduced in very many laboratories for two decades, and they opened a door: a solid-state quantum system that can be read out and controlled in ambient conditions, which is the basis for nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and strain sensing, and for spin registers used in network experiments. Three colleagues who do not rank it first (Johansson, Kroll, Eriksson) said in round 1 that a Wrachtrup and Jelezko pair is the cleaner attribution if B001 is considered, and nobody disputed that the physics is real. I therefore propose a citation limited to detection and coherent control of the single spin, so that it does not claim the later quantum-register and sensing programme.
statement.case_against: I remain the only member who prefers B001, and I will not treat my first place as evidence of wider support. The case against is real. First, Mehlig asks what physics was discovered, as opposed to a tool being made; my answer is that single-spin detection and control in a solid at room temperature is a new quantum behaviour made observable, but the committee may judge it an enabling technique. Second, Hanson, Awschalom and others followed the original experiments quickly, and the field's identity is now quantum sensing, where a two-name prize looks narrow and Lukin's role is larger. Third, biological and clinical sensing claims are still developing, so on benefit to humanity this is weaker than a clock with a pending redefinition of the second. Fourth, I recall the 1997 and 2004 priority details from memory and want them checked against the record before a vote.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B029 first and answered my novelty concern by saying that the 2005 prize recognised the comb and the 2012 prize control of single ions, while neither covered a many-atom magic-wavelength lattice reaching 10^-18, a different route past the quantum-projection-noise limit of a single ion. He also agreed that a Wrachtrup and Jelezko pair would be the cleaner attribution for B001.
responses.response: That answer moves me partway. I accept that a many-atom lattice clock is a physically distinct route, and I withdraw the stronger version of my objection that the territory has simply been honoured. I still hold that the part of the case that rests on the original experiment is a two-step story, the magic-wavelength proposal and then the long engineering of 10^-18 systematics in several laboratories, and the committee must be sure that Katori and Ye are the people for both steps, since Lemonde, Peik and Hollberg proposed a similar scheme and many groups share the achievement. On benefit I am not fully persuaded that redefinition of the second is near enough to count, but I agree it is not a reason to reject B029 and I keep it as my first alternative. If an outside assessment of the proposal history is requested, as the chair suggests, I would support it.

responses.point: Mehlig finds the NV work scientifically solid and well reproduced but mainly a tool and sensor, and he wants a clearer statement of what physics it discovered before ranking it above a new regime of correlated matter such as magic-angle graphene. He also holds that Bistritzer must stay in B031 because he is first author of the prediction.
responses.response: The distinction between a tool and a discovery is the right test and I take it seriously. My answer is that observing one electron spin in a solid with light, and showing that its quantum state can be driven coherently at room temperature, was not expected to work and was shown by experiment first, so I count it as a discovery that is also an invention, which is what the Physics Prize has often rewarded. Where I agree with you is that B031 is a strong second choice for me, because a prediction followed by a decisive experiment fits my criterion. My difficulty is the same one you named: the unresolved pairing mechanism, the omission of Cao and Fatemi, and a field under ten years old. If B031 were to be chosen, I would prefer that the committee say openly why it credits Bistritzer rather than leave this implicit, and I accept your point that the three-name set follows prediction plus leading experimental group.

responses.point: Johansson said he found my attribution argument convincing, that single-NV detection and control are the discovery and that Lukin's later register and sensing work builds on it, and that Wrachtrup and Jelezko is the defensible pair; he still ranks B004 above B001 on novelty, and he has flagged a possible recusal on B004.
responses.response: I thank you for that and I note that your own case for circuit QED is serious. On your recusal question, I think it is for the chair to decide, but I would support you stepping back from B004 discussion and any ballot on it, with Kroll's WACQT link handled in the same way if B004 becomes decisive, because we both know how close institutional ties at Chalmers are, and I say this as your colleague at the same university. On substance, I would not put B001 above B004 on novelty either; where we differ is that I find the single-spin experiments more directly verified and less tied to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits. I also understand your position that B004 has a four-names-for-three-places problem, and I do not think that can be solved by anyone on this committee from the record we have.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B031 first, would not oppose a two-name version of B001, and said that Lukin should only be added if the committee frames the citation around quantum sensing as a field, since otherwise the credit belongs with the original detection and control experiments.
responses.response: We agree on the logic: the citation decides the names. If the committee frames it as the original detection and coherent control of a single spin, the names are Wrachtrup and Jelezko; if it frames it as quantum sensing, Lukin and probably Hanson and Awschalom enter and the three-person limit becomes a problem I do not think we can solve fairly. I therefore keep the narrow framing. On B031 I accept your separation of the discovery from the mechanism, and I accept that superconductivity discoveries have been honoured before the mechanism was known. My remaining concern is device-to-device variability and the unlisted experimental co-authors; I would like the experimentalists on the committee to say how many independent groups have seen the superconducting phase.

uncertainties: Exact priority and division of credit between the 1997 single-centre optical detection and the 2004 coherent control, including the roles of Gruber and other co-authors; I recall these from memory and they should be checked in the record before a final ballot.

Whether the committee will accept a narrow citation on single-spin detection and control or instead insist on a quantum-sensing framing that would bring in Lukin, Hanson and Awschalom and strain the three-person limit.

Whether B029 is the stronger candidate on experimental maturity and number of independent laboratories; I regard that as likely, and my choice of B001 over it depends on novelty and not on confidence in the clocks.
Whether B031 is mature enough given the unsettled pairing mechanism, device variability and the omitted experimentalists.
statement.conflict_note: I have no known collaboration with Wrachtrup, Jelezko, Lukin, Hanson, Awschalom or the credited names on B029 and B031. I share Chalmers with Göran Johansson, who has flagged B004, and I support the chair deciding that he step back from B004 and that Kroll's WACQT overlap be noted if B004 is considered. This does not touch B001. As an electron microscopist I have a general sympathy for instrument-driven discoveries, which may bias me toward B001, and I state it for the record.
